habitat: Dense lush thickets and rank herbaceous growth, usually away from water, including woodland edge and tangled undergrowth.
summary: A small plain Palearctic warbler of thickets rather than reedbeds. Adults are olive-brown above, including a yellowish-brown rump that is not rufous, with a short creamy eyebrow and buffy-white underparts washed yellowish. The sexes look alike. First-year birds are warmer brown and may show a rufous tinge on the rump. The colour of a newly hatched chick is not described in the texts used here. A published total length was not in the texts used here.

similar.note: Common Reed Warbler keeps more to reeds, is warmer brown, and has a rufous rump. Silent birds need in-hand measurements; the songs differ, and Marsh Warbler mimics other species.
Icterine Warbler is yellower below when fresh and shows a pale panel on the closed wing. It also uses the tree canopy more.

bill.shape: shorter and stronger than Common Reed Warbler, with a steeper forehead; the lower mandible is pale yellowish-horn or flesh

underparts.pattern: buffy-white and washed yellowish, with darker flanks

viewNotes.note: Plain olive-brown upperparts. The rump is tinged yellowish-brown and is not rufous. No pale wing panel is described.
Underwing-coverts are yellowish-buff. The underside of the flight feathers is not separately described.
A short creamy eyebrow and thin creamy eye-ring, with a white or creamy throat and a yellowish wash on the breast.
Olive-brown mantle and a yellowish-brown rump, with a blackish-brown tail. Fresh plumage is more olive-green on the head.
A small olive-brown warbler with pinkish legs and a short eyebrow, usually in thicket rather than in a reed stem. The forehead is steeper than on Common Reed Warbler.
First-year birds are warmer brown and may have a rufous tinge on the rump, so they can look like a reed warbler.

calls.description: The male’s song imitates other birds, on average about 75 species, learned in the hatching summer and the first winter in Africa.

Females may give a simple song without imitation; the texts used here do not describe that song beyond saying it lacks mimicry. This grade B cut from Sweden has two singers. The recordist interprets the second singer, heard after the parabola turns at 0:55, as the female, and the first as the male. It was contributed to the female bird song project.

research.note: Status is palearctic-migrant. Months are November–April from Raijmakers and SABAP1, which says arrival is mostly in December and departure is in April. SABAP1 also says it sings on the non-breeding grounds. No total length was published in the texts used here; Raijmakers gives wing 60–76 mm. No grade-A recording is labelled as a female. The female song is grade B from Sweden, and the female is the recordist’s interpretation of the second singer. The male song used is grade A from the Eastern Cape. A sharp Kruger photograph was not used because the only candidate was too blurred to show the marks. Chick down is not described.
